questions.learningObjective: Explain what a recurring set of six line-end words establishes in a sestina.
questions.stem: The marine biologist's log lists six recurring words at the end of each stanza. Explain what that pattern establishes.

answer.exemplar: The six words are the end-words of a sestina, and repeating them at the end of every line gives the poem a fixed set of terms that never leave. The reader begins to hear relations among them that no single line states, so the words gather a charge of meaning across the six stanzas. By the end they carry the argument between them rather than simply decorating the lines.

questions.explanation: The end-words of a sestina recur in a fixed order at the ends of successive lines. Because the same six words keep returning, the reader builds relations between them that accumulate into the poem's argument.
questions.hint: Count what returns at every line ending.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a monologue establishes a speaker with a history.
questions.stem: Explain how the tank log's verse establishes a speaker with a history.

answer.exemplar: The poem establishes its speaker through what the speaker assumes the listener already knows. References to an earlier feeding, to the cover that was moved last winter, and to the keeper's habit of arriving late all presuppose a shared past between the two of them. That presumption is what gives the speech its depth: the reader hears a history being invoked rather than a life being explained from the beginning, which is one of the pleasures of the form.

questions.explanation: A dramatic monologue builds depth through shared assumptions rather than biography. References to earlier feedings, a moved cover and the keeper's habits presuppose a shared past, so the speech carries history without narrating it.

answer.exemplar: The repeated line works as a refrain, and a refrain fixes a phrase in the reader's memory so that each return carries the weight of the last one. questions.learningObjective: Explain how a sestina reaches a conclusion without stating it.
questions.stem: Which claim best explains how the log's sestina argues its case?

options.text: It states the case plainly in its first stanza and then illustrates it with images.
options.misconception: describes the sestina as an illustrated thesis

options.text: It relies on the reader's knowledge of marine biology to complete the meaning.
options.misconception: attributes the argument to outside expertise

options.text: It puts its six terms into changing combinations, so the reader draws the conclusion itself.
It argues by the accumulated weight of many images rather than by structure.
options.misconception: credits sheer imagery rather than form

questions.explanation: A sestina argues by arrangement: the same terms are recombined until their relations make the case for the reader. The conclusion comes from what the reader notices between the words, not from a statement.
questions.hint: Ask who draws the conclusion.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the part of a sestina that completes its cycle of end-words.
questions.stem: In the log's sestina, which part of the poem completes the cycle of the end-words?

options.text: The final stanza, because it restores the opening order of the six end-words.
The first stanza, because the poem must end where it began in every sense.
options.misconception: confuses the closing order with a general symmetry

options.text: The tercet, because the middle of a sestina is where the order is finally settled.
options.misconception: locates the resolution in the middle of the poem

options.text: The envoi, because the closing address is where the words are counted one last time.
options.misconception: invents a counting function for an envoi

questions.explanation: The final stanza restores the opening order of the end-words, completing the cycle the poem has been running. Only the closing stanza can do it, since the permutation moves forward from every earlier arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask which stanza ends the rotation.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the form that recurs in six end-words from the form that repeats two lines.
questions.stem: The marine biologist's notes offer a rotating set of six recurring words. Which form uses them?

options.text: A villanelle, because it repeats two lines rather than six individual words.
options.misconception: confuses the villanelle with the sestina

options.text: A dramatic monologue, because a single speaker can use any vocabulary he likes.
options.misconception: treats vocabulary choice as evidence of a form

options.text: A sestina, because six terms recur at the ends of successive lines in a fixed order.
A prose poem, because recurring words only matter when there are no line breaks.
options.misconception: ties the recurrence of words to the absence of lines

questions.explanation: Six recurring terms, placed at the ends of successive lines and moved by a fixed rule, belong to a sestina. A villanelle repeats two complete lines instead, so the difference is one of what is repeated.
questions.hint: Count what recurs: two lines or six words?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a monologue needs its listener rather than only its subject.
questions.stem: Explain why the tank log's monologue needs its listener rather than its subject.

answer.exemplar: The subject of the log's poem could be described in a note; it is the listener who makes the poem necessary. Because the eel is speaking to the keeper who has fed it and ignored it, every claim it makes is measured against that relationship, and the reader has to judge what can be asked of a creature in that position. Without an addressee the speech would collapse into description, and the whole ethical weight of the passage would go with it.

questions.explanation: The subject of the poem could be described in a note; the listener is what makes it a poem. Because the eel speaks to the keeper who has fed and ignored it, every claim is measured against that relationship.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker needs from the listener.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Assess the claim that a logged monologue is only a set of notes.
questions.stem: Assess the claim that the log's monologue is only a set of notes.

options.text: The claim holds, because a scientific log should contain nothing but measurements.
options.misconception: insists a log may only contain measurements

options.text: The claim holds, since notes are short and the poem runs across several pages.
options.misconception: judges by length rather than by purpose

options.text: The claim fails, but only because the poem is written in lines rather than prose.
options.misconception: grounds the distinction in surface form

options.text: The claim fails, because a sustained address to a listener with a shared history is not a note's purpose.

questions.explanation: A note records information; this poem argues with someone whose judgement the speaker cares about. That sustained address, with its shared references and its need for a reply, is a different kind of writing from a record.
questions.hint: Ask what the writing is trying to achieve.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a recurring set of line-ending terms and the form it implies.

stimulus.body: A stanza is printed with the words that close each line: 'net', 'wet', 'set', 'bet', 'jet', 'get'. The biologist notes that this is the fourth time she has used this group of words, and that each time they have closed a stanza about nets and currents.

questions.stem: The tank log records the end-words of a stanza. What does the sequence show?

options.text: That the poem is a villanelle, since the same two refrains recur in every stanza.
options.misconception: counts six recurring words as two refrains

options.text: That the poem is a sestina, since the same six end-words recur from stanza to stanza.
That the words were chosen only because they are easy to rhyme together.
options.misconception: reduces the choice to rhyme convenience

options.text: That the stanza has been copied from the biologist's own earlier writing.
options.misconception: infers copying from repeated vocabulary

questions.explanation: The same six terms recurring at line ends, stanza after stanza, are the end-words of a sestina. The note about their use in stanzas about nets confirms the recurrence is structural rather than a coincidence of subject.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same group keeps returning.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how recombining a fixed vocabulary produces an argument.
questions.stem: Explain how a permutation of end-words becomes an argument in the tank log.

options.text: Because the reader must already know marine biology to follow the argument at all.
options.misconception: credits outside expertise for the poem's case

options.text: Because the same six terms meet in new combinations, their relations keep making and unmaking the case.
Because the sestina is a form that was invented for arguments of this kind.
options.misconception: attributes the argument to the form's origin

options.text: Because the repetition of six words is enough to make any set of words into an argument.
options.misconception: claims repetition alone produces an argument

questions.explanation: A permutation argues by recombination. The same six terms keep meeting in changed company, so the reader watches relations form and dissolve, and that shifting pattern is where the case is made.
questions.hint: Ask what keeps changing between stanzas.
